# env / t3-env

Type-safe environment variables via [`@t3-oss/env-nextjs`](https://env.t3.gg/).
Validates at boot, fails loudly on missing or malformed values.

This is the **reference slot item** — agents authoring new registry packages
should look here first. It demonstrates:

- `slot` + `variant` in the manifest (`env` + `t3-env`).
- `{{scope}}` placeholder usage in the source.
- `dependencies` declared as bare specs (catalog-merged).
- `environment: "universal"` (the code touches `process.env` but t3-env
  guards against tree-shaking it on the client side).
- A `docs` paragraph that tells the user **exactly what to do next**.

## What it scaffolds

```
packages/env/
  package.json         # generated from the manifest (name, deps, exports)
  tsconfig.json        # generated from environment + lib hints
  src/
    index.ts           # this file, with {{scope}} substituted
```

## After install

Set the values listed in `.env.example` (the file `cts` appended on
install) inside a real `.env.local` at the repo root. The validated env is
then available anywhere:

```ts
import { env } from "@scope/env";

if (env.NODE_ENV === "production") {
  // ...
}
```

## Adding env vars from another package

When another slot item (say `auth/better-auth`) needs `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`,
it declares that key in its own manifest's `envVars`. The resolver merges
all `envVars` across the selected items and the generated `env` package's
`createEnv` schema gains them automatically — you do not edit this file by
hand to add them.

## Why not just `process.env`?

`process.env` is `Record<string, string | undefined>` — every read is a
nullable string. Validating once at boot turns it into a typed object, and
catches "I forgot to set this in production" at startup instead of at
3:14 a.m. when the first user hits the bad code path.
